text:
Nearby residents express frustration as visitors surge to Aegibong Peace Ecopark More than 13,000 people visited Aegibong Peace Ecopark in Gimpo, Gyeonggi Province, over a 10-day period, to catch a rare glimpse of a North Korean self-propelled howitzer visible from the observatory.
Despite the heightened tensions between the two Koreas, a total of 13,243 people visited the park from Oct. 26 to Nov. 4, up 7.5 percent from 12,321 during the same period last year, according to Gimpo city, Sunday.
The increase came after images published by local media showing a North Korean self-propelled howitzer stationed along the North Korean coast, about 1.5 kilometers from the observatory, went viral.
Weekday visits rose sharply, with daily number of visitors reaching 1,000 to 1,200, up as much as 35 percent from a year earlier. Weekend attendance, however, fell nearly 10 percent to 4,200 due to entry restrictions, as the park is currently limiting the number of visitors on-site to 500 at a time for safety reasons.
The artillery is close enough to be seen through binoculars and telescopes from the observatory. However, North Korean troops recently covered the weapon with camouflage netting, making it difficult to identify, according to city officials.
As more visitors flock to the park, Gimpo has gradually reduced the number of advance reservations spots. Since Wednesday, reservations have been limited to 200 people per hour, 100 slots to individual visitors and another 100 to groups.
However, the influx sparked frustration among some nearby residents, who say visitors are treating a source of daily security anxiety as a tourist attraction.
"With North Korean artillery pointing in our direction, we live each day fearing that shelling could happen at any moment," a resident of Wolgot-myeon in Gimpo was quoted as saying by Yonhap News Agency on condition of anonymity.
"For us, this is a matter of survival, but it is upsetting to see outsiders treating it as a mere spectacle," the resident said.
The resident also expressed concern over North Korea's threats regarding propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts toward the South, saying that only those who have experienced such tensions can understand the distress they cause.
"I sincerely hope inter-Korean tensions will ease as soon as possible," the resident added.
A Gimpo city official said the park was made to help visitors confront the reality of the division of the Korean Peninsula and reflect on the value of peace.
"Even if people initially visit out of simple curiosity, we hope the experience will encourage them to take a greater interest in peace and better understand the difficulties faced by local residents," the official said.
